messages.subject: openCR and very large dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I am trying to use openCR in R Studio to estimate the changes in abundance over time for boodies (Bettongia lesueur). I’ve been handed a lot of legacy data to do this and currently have my capthist file coded with 23 sessions and 123 occasions with some 970 trap locations, most of which are not open in any given occasion. I’ve managed to plot my capthist file but when I try to use spatial analysis I’m getting to following error:

> spatial2<-openCR.fit(BL,detectfn='HHN',mask=mask.clipped,type='JSSAsecrl',method="Newton-Raphson")

Error in table(df$newID, df$newocc, df$newtrap, useNA = "no") :

  attempt to make a table with >= 2^31 elements

Non-spatial analysis is giving me a lot of NAs and values that make no sense and there is no variation among sessions. Closed population analyses worked great.

I’ve tried limiting my dataset to just the final 2 sessions of capture data and the various spatial secr models work, so I’m guessing that Dr Efford’s suggestion that my dataset is just too big for an all-inclusive analysis using openCR as it is programmed at present is correct.

My question is; will using a super computer overcome this issue or is it a limit within the openCR code? If the limit is within openCR will the software DENSITY be able to process a dataset of this size? Can anyone give me a limit on the number of sessions, occasions, and trap points that these programs can process?

I would appreciate any advice people can give me regarding the analysis of large legacy datasets.

Thanks,

Cheryl

messages.subject: Re: openCR and very large dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I'm not ready to give a definitive answer on this, but note -

The R error will happen even on a supercomputer.

DENSITY has its own limits and only does some closed population analyses, so don't go there.

I am surprised you hit 2^31, as the product of number of animals x number of occasions x number of detectors doesn't seem to get near that. Maybe there is a problem in the way you specified things.

How to deal with long studies is an open research question - I have toyed with a moving-window approach for a long possum dataset (79 sessions) implemented in openCR as 'moving.fit' but can't yet recommend that as it's not fully documented and gives different results to a unified analysis.

Murray

messages.subject: secr for semi-closed boundaries
messages.body_plain: Hi. I am working with brown hyaena data in South Africa. The camera trap grids are in three different types of area - completely open (no fences; free movement), completely closed (impenetrable fences that are heavily maintained; no movement outside the reserve), and semi-closed (fenced areas that have penetrable holes that appear for awhile, holes are periodically closed up by rangers, new holes appear and these are closed, etc; restricted movement outside the reserve). In semi-closed areas, brown hyaenas can move in and out of the reserve (and predators do) but movement is not as easy as a completely open area. I suspect that if all other conditions were the same, density in a semi-closed area may be higher than a completely open area but not as high as a completely closed area. Do you think this is the case? I know how to run estimates for completely open areas and completely closed areas, but I was wondering if there is a technique in secr to accurately estimate density in a semi-closed area? If not, should I just run the semi-closed areas as if they were completely open (with an appropriate statespace that isn't restricted to the fenceline)? Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: secr for semi-closed boundaries
messages.body_plain:
There's no technique in secr that addresses this directly, at least as I understand the problem. I don't think we can answer the question about likely density differences without knowledge of the system - presumably there are gradients in prey density as well as fence effects and mysteries of hyaena behaviour.

As I understand it the holes are ephemeral and not documented, and that rules out directly modeling them using non-euclidean distance methods. Under a completely closed scenario all captures inside are of animals with activity centres inside, but under a partly closed scenario some may be intruders. How to measure the magnitude of this effect? I can't see that captures from only inside give any information on the fraction of animals that are intruders so you would have to infer that from other information (or guess it). One way to adjust the modelled proportion of intruders might be to impose a zero-density buffer around the reserve (i.e. drop an annulus of pixels from the habitat mask); the width of that buffer would control the frequency of incursion. But as there is no information on that frequency we're back to square one.

Sorry not to be more helpful.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: openCR and very large dataset
messages.body_plain:
>From files that Cheryl sent privately I can see that part of the problem is a misunderstanding over the numbering of occasions and sessions. Occasions should always be numbered with consecutive integers 1, 2... within a session. In this dataset there are 3-9 occasions per session, not 123.

In openCR a multisession secr capthist object will be collapsed with join() to a single session, concatenating and renumbering the occasions. This is what you anticipated by providing 'usage' data for all 123 occasions in the trap file. It should 'work' (read the data) if you replace the 'session' column of the input capture file with a constant and manually assign a vector of intervals to define the primary sessions.

However, the problem is still too large for openCR.fit, at least on my machine, and something must be done to cut it down. 970 detector locations x 930 animals x 123 occasions just demands too much memory.

Murray
